cards.front: How do tetracyclines stop bacterial growth, and why are they selectively toxic to bacteria?
cards.back: They are mainly bacteriostatic. They bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and stop aminoacyl-tRNA from reaching the acceptor site, so the peptide chain cannot grow. Susceptible bacteria concentrate them by an energy-dependent active transport system that host cells lack, and host ribosomes are less sensitive.

cards.front: Classify the tetracyclines in clinical use.
cards.text: Clinically relevant tetracyclines are {{tetracycline}}, {{oxytetracycline}}, {{demeclocycline}}, {{doxycycline}} and {{minocycline}}; the glycylcycline {{tigecycline}} is a newer synthetic subclass member.

cards.front: Why is doxycycline preferred over the older tetracyclines?
cards.back: It is almost completely absorbed whether or not food is present. Older agents need an empty stomach, and calcium, iron, milk, antacids and sucralfate bind them. Doxycycline is excreted mainly in faeces, so it can be used in renal failure, and the usual dose is 100 mg once or twice daily. Enzyme inducers such as phenobarbitone, carbamazepine and phenytoin shorten its half-life.

cards.front: What distinguishes minocycline from the other tetracyclines?
cards.back: It is the most lipid-soluble and most potent member, and it accumulates in body fat. It is mainly metabolised, not excreted by the kidney. Its distinctive toxicity is vestibular (ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus), which settles after stopping. It remains active against some meningococci and has useful activity against M. leprae.

cards.front: Which sexually transmitted and atypical infections are first-line for tetracyclines?
cards.text: {{Chlamydial}} urethritis and cervicitis (doxycycline for 7 days); {{lymphogranuloma venereum}}; {{granuloma inguinale}} (about 3 weeks); {{Mycoplasma}} pneumonia and {{psittacosis}}; cholera as an {{adjunct}} that reduces stool volume.

cards.front: Which rickettsial, zoonotic and other serious infections are first-line tetracycline targets?
cards.back: Rickettsial diseases (typhus, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Q fever) respond dramatically. Brucellosis: doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks, with gentamicin added in acute cases. Plague (bubonic and pneumonic) and relapsing fever also respond, and tetracyclines are favoured for mass treatment in an epidemic, although streptomycin acts faster.

cards.front: Tigecycline: what is special about it, and where is it not used?
cards.back: A glycylcycline derived from minocycline that is active against many tetracycline-resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including MRSA and VRE, because the usual tetracycline efflux pumps and ribosomal protection do not work against it. It is given only by slow i.v. infusion and is approved for severe community-acquired pneumonia, complicated skin infections and complicated intra-abdominal infections. Not used for hospital-acquired or ventilator pneumonia (higher mortality), for urinary infection, or in children and pregnancy. Pseudomonas and Proteus are inherently resistant.

cards.front: How does chloramphenicol act, and how does its spectrum differ from tetracyclines?
cards.back: It binds the 50S ribosome near the acceptor site and blocks peptide bond formation, while aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the 30S unit is unaffected. It is mainly bacteriostatic. Compared with tetracyclines it is more active against H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, B. pertussis and B. fragilis, and less active against gram-positive cocci and spirochaetes.

cards.front: Chloramphenicol: classify its bone marrow toxicity.
cards.text: Dose-related marrow suppression is {{predictable}} and usually {{reversible}}; the idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia is rare (about 1 in {{40,000}}), often fatal, probably genetic, and survivors may later develop {{leukaemia}}.

cards.front: What is grey baby syndrome, and when does it occur?
cards.back: A toxic reaction to chloramphenicol given at high doses (about 100 mg/kg), mainly prophylactically to premature or newborn infants. Their liver cannot conjugate the drug and their kidney cannot clear it well. Features: feeding refusal, vomiting, hypotonia, hypothermia, abdominal distension, irregular breathing and ashen grey cyanosis, progressing to circulatory collapse and death. Blood lactate rises. Chloramphenicol should be avoided in neonates.

cards.front: What are the important drug interactions of chloramphenicol?
cards.back: It inhibits hepatic metabolism of warfarin, phenytoin and cyclophosphamide, raising their levels. Enzyme inducers (phenobarbitone, phenytoin, rifampicin) speed up chloramphenicol metabolism, so therapeutic failure can occur.

cards.front: How does tetracycline affect teeth and bone, and does the timing of exposure matter?
cards.back: Calcium-tetracycline chelate is deposited in developing teeth and bone. Exposure from mid-pregnancy to about 5 months after birth causes brown discolouration and malformed deciduous teeth that are prone to caries. Exposure from about 3 months to 6 years affects the crowns of permanent anterior teeth, and repeated courses are worse. Late pregnancy or childhood exposure can temporarily suppress bone growth.

cards.front: In which situations should tetracyclines be avoided or used with caution?
cards.text: Avoid tetracyclines in {{pregnancy}}, {{lactation}} and {{children}}; avoid with {{diuretics}} (blood urea rises); caution in renal or hepatic insufficiency; never mix injectable tetracycline with {{penicillin}}.

cards.front: How do aminoglycosides kill bacteria?
cards.back: They must first cross the cell wall and cytoplasmic membrane by an oxygen-dependent, energy-driven transport, which is why anaerobes are not affected. Inside, they bind 30S ribosomes (others also bind 50S and the interface), freeze initiation, break up polysomes and cause misreading of the mRNA code. Faulty proteins damage the membrane, causing leakage and cell death, so the action is bactericidal.

cards.front: Summarise the pharmacokinetics of systemically given aminoglycosides.
cards.back: Highly ionised, so not absorbed orally; given i.m. or i.v., with peak levels in 30 to 60 minutes. They distribute only in extracellular fluid (volume about 0.3 L/kg), reach poor levels in CSF and aqueous humour, and high levels in the renal cortex and endolymph, which explains their toxicity. Not metabolised; excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration. Half-life 2 to 4 hours, prolonged in renal failure, the elderly and neonates. They cross the placenta.

cards.front: Why are aminoglycosides increasingly given once daily?
cards.back: They kill in a concentration-dependent way and have a long post-antibiotic effect, so a single high dose works as well as divided doses. Lower levels for longer each day let drug wash out of the endolymph and renal cortex, so single daily dosing is less nephrotoxic with equal efficacy, and it is cheaper. No regimen is less ototoxic than another. Avoid extended-interval dosing in renal insufficiency, in children, and when a beta-lactam is combined for endocarditis.

cards.front: How is an aminoglycoside dose adjusted for reduced renal function?
cards.back: Renal clearance parallels creatinine clearance (about two-thirds of it), so no reduction is needed while CLcr is above about 70 mL/min. Below that, reduce the daily dose or lengthen the interval according to measured CLcr. Elderly patients and neonates accumulate the drug, so they need the same adjustment.

cards.front: Gentamicin: why is it important, what is the usual dose, and how is it combined?
cards.back: It is the prototype and most widely used systemic aminoglycoside. Dose 3 to 5 mg/kg/day, given once daily or divided, i.m. or slow i.v. over 30 to 60 minutes. It covers aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Serratia, Pseudomonas) and some staphylococci, but not streptococci or enterococci on its own. It synergises with penicillin, ampicillin or vancomycin in enterococcal endocarditis and with a beta-lactam in Pseudomonas meningitis. It should not be used for community-acquired pneumonia.

cards.front: What is streptomycin used for today?
cards.back: Its use is now limited because of resistance, lower potency and toxicity. In TB it was a first-line drug in older regimens (KDT), but GG14 notes that streptomycin and the other injectables have largely been dropped from TB regimens because of irreversible ototoxicity and vestibular damage. Other uses: plague (rapid cure, alone or with a tetracycline), tularaemia (drug of choice), and with penicillin in subacute bacterial endocarditis. It is the least nephrotoxic aminoglycoside, but vestibular damage is common.

cards.front: Amikacin: why is it kept in reserve?
cards.back: A semisynthetic kanamycin derivative that resists most aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes, so it covers many gentamicin- and tobramycin-resistant Gram-negative bacilli. It is reserved for hospital-acquired Gram-negative infection where local sensitivity shows resistance to gentamicin or tobramycin. Dose 15 mg/kg/day. Its toxicity is more cochlear than vestibular. In MDR-TB it was a standard injectable in older regimens (KDT); GG14 places it in WHO Group C, used only when a regimen cannot be built from Group A and B drugs.

cards.front: Tobramycin: how does it differ from gentamicin?
cards.back: Its spectrum, pharmacokinetics and dose (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) are almost identical to gentamicin, but it is 2 to 4 times more active against Pseudomonas and Proteus. Many gentamicin-resistant strains are cross-resistant, though some remain sensitive. It is not used with penicillin for enterococcal endocarditis; its main use is serious Pseudomonas and Proteus infection, as an alternative to gentamicin.

cards.front: Classify the gut-acting aminoglycosides and their uses.
cards.text: Oral {{neomycin}} is used for {{bowel preparation}} before surgery and for {{hepatic encephalopathy}}; {{paromomycin}} is given orally for intestinal {{amoebiasis}} and {{giardiasis}}. Neither is absorbed, but systemic use of neomycin is avoided because of {{ototoxicity}} and {{nephrotoxicity}}.

cards.front: How do bacteria become resistant to aminoglycosides, and which mechanism matters most?
cards.back: Most important: plasmid-encoded enzymes that phosphorylate, adenylate or acetylate the drug. The modified drug no longer binds ribosomes or enters cells well. These plasmids are common in hospital organisms and can carry multidrug resistance. Less common: mutation of ribosomal proteins, and reduced uptake. Cross-resistance is variable because enzyme susceptibility differs; amikacin resists most of these enzymes.

cards.front: Describe the two types of aminoglycoside ototoxicity and which drugs favour each.
cards.back: Cochlear: damage starts at the base of the cochlea, so high frequencies are lost first. It is often silent until audiometry, then tinnitus and permanent hearing loss, because hair cells do not regenerate. Kanamycin and amikacin are most cochlear. Vestibular: headache, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, ataxia and nystagmus. Partial recovery occurs over 1 to 2 years. Streptomycin and gentamicin are more vestibular.

cards.front: How does aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity appear, and what increases the risk?
cards.back: Proximal tubular damage: loss of urinary concentrating power, low GFR, nitrogen retention, albuminuria and casts. The drug accumulates in the renal cortex, so toxicity tracks total dose and duration. Risk is higher in the elderly and in pre-existing kidney disease. Single daily dosing is less toxic. Damage is reversible if the drug is stopped promptly. Reduced clearance raises levels and worsens ototoxicity. Streptomycin is the least nephrotoxic.

cards.front: How is gentamicin monitored to limit toxicity?
cards.back: By the trough plasma concentration. Vestibular damage becomes concentration-dependent above about 2 mcg/mL, so dosing should keep the measured trough below 1 mcg/mL. Dose by renal function.

cards.front: Which drugs add to aminoglycoside toxicity?
cards.text: Additive nephrotoxicity: {{amphotericin B}}, {{vancomycin}}, {{cyclosporine}}, {{cisplatin}} and {{NSAIDs}}. Additive ototoxicity (use cautiously): {{furosemide}} and {{minocycline}}.

cards.front: When should aminoglycosides be avoided even though they are otherwise indicated?
cards.back: Pregnancy: they cross the placenta and can cause hearing loss in the baby; streptomycin is contraindicated. Perforated eardrum: aminoglycoside ear drops can cause ototoxicity. Myasthenia gravis: they accentuate the weakness by adding to neuromuscular block. Neomycin is contraindicated when renal function is impaired.

cards.front: Short note: Toxicity of aminoglycosides

Kanamycin and amikacin mainly cochlear; streptomycin and gentamicin mainly vestibular
Proximal tubular injury; reversible if stopped early
Risk rises with high total dose, age and existing renal disease
Reduced ACh release; dangerous after intraperitoneal or pleural instillation with curare-like drugs
Reversed by i.v. calcium; neostigmine response inconsistent
Gentamicin trough below 1 mcg/mL
Once-daily dosing adjusted to CLcr
Avoid in pregnancy and with other nephrotoxins

cards.front: How does erythromycin act, and which organisms does it cover?
cards.back: It binds the 50S ribosome and blocks translocation of the growing peptide from the A site back to the P site. The ribosome stalls, and larger proteins are prematurely terminated. It is mainly bacteriostatic. Its narrow spectrum covers Gram-positive cocci (streptococci, pneumococci), Clostridia, C. diphtheriae, Listeria, plus Campylobacter, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Gardnerella. Enterobacteriaceae and B. fragilis are not covered.

cards.front: What are the main mechanisms of macrolide resistance, and what cross-resistance follows?
cards.back: Efflux pumps in cocci; plasmid-encoded methylase that alters the ribosomal binding site (the most important mechanism in Gram-positives); erythromycin esterase in enterobacteria; chromosomal 50S mutation in some. Resistance extends to other macrolides, and partly to clindamycin and chloramphenicol, whose ribosomal binding sites lie close together.

cards.front: Why is erythromycin dangerous with terfenadine, astemizole or cisapride?
cards.back: Erythromycin (and clarithromycin) inhibits CYP3A4, raising levels of the co-prescribed drug. Terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride then cause QT prolongation, serious ventricular arrhythmias and death, and these drugs were withdrawn. Erythromycin also raises levels of theophylline, carbamazepine, valproate, ergotamine and warfarin. Azithromycin interacts much less.

cards.front: Which erythromycin ester causes cholestatic hepatitis, and when does it appear?
cards.back: The lauryl sulfate estolate. It causes hepatitis with cholestatic jaundice, resembling viral hepatitis or biliary obstruction, usually after 1 to 3 weeks. Pregnancy increases the risk. It is probably a hypersensitivity reaction and clears on stopping. Rarely seen with the ethylsuccinate or stearate esters. Erythromycin base or another ester can be given later without recurrence.

cards.front: What makes azithromycin preferable to erythromycin, and how should it be taken?
cards.back: It is acid-stable, better tolerated and has fewer CYP3A4 interactions. Tissue and intracellular concentrations are high, and the terminal half-life exceeds 50 hours, so short courses work once daily. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after food, because food reduces absorption. It is excreted mainly in bile, with little renal excretion. The child dose is 10 mg/kg/day.

cards.front: Which sexually transmitted infections are treated with azithromycin, and at what regimen?
cards.text: Urogenital chlamydia: {{single 1 g dose}}; chancroid and PPNG: {{single 1 g dose}}; lymphogranuloma venereum: {{1 g weekly for 3 weeks}}; donovanosis: {{500 mg daily for 7 days}} or 1 g weekly for 4 weeks; Legionnaires pneumonia: {{500 mg daily for 2 weeks}}.

cards.front: Classify the newer macrolides and name one key feature of each.
cards.text: {{Clarithromycin}} inhibits CYP3A4 and is used in H. pylori triple therapy and MAC infection; {{roxithromycin}} has a long half-life for twice daily dosing; {{telithromycin}} is a ketolide restricted because of hepatitis; {{azithromycin}} is an azalide given once daily; {{spiramycin}} limits transplacental toxoplasmosis.

cards.front: Clindamycin: mechanism, spectrum and where it is most useful.
cards.back: A lincosamide that binds the 50S ribosome like erythromycin, with partial cross-resistance: a constitutive ribosomal methylase confers resistance to both, while an inducible one may allow selection of resistant staphylococci during therapy. It covers most streptococci, penicillinase-producing staphylococci and most anaerobes, especially Bacteroides fragilis. KDT lists it as inactive against MRSA, but GG14 notes it is useful for oral treatment of skin infections where MRSA is a possible pathogen. It is inactive against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, enterococci, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Rickettsia. It penetrates bone well but not the CSF. Because it inhibits toxin production, GG14 recommends it as an adjunct in toxin-mediated streptococcal and staphylococcal infection.

cards.front: What is the most serious adverse effect of clindamycin, and how is it managed?
cards.back: Antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis from Clostridioides difficile overgrowth, which can be fatal; clindamycin carries one of the highest risks of this among antibiotics. Stop the drug at once. KDT gives oral metronidazole as first choice and oral vancomycin as the alternative; GG14 states that oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are now preferred, with metronidazole only for non-severe disease, and i.v. metronidazole added to oral vancomycin in fulminant disease. Clindamycin is therefore reserved for anaerobic and mixed infections and for skin infection in penicillin-allergic patients. Other effects include rash and rarely raised liver enzymes.

cards.front: How does vancomycin kill bacteria, and how do enterococci resist it?
cards.back: It binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors, so they cannot be polymerised and cross-linked, and the cell wall weakens. It acts only on Gram-positive bacteria; Gram-negative bacilli and mycobacteria are resistant. It is not absorbed orally. Enterococci resist (VRE) through van gene clusters that change the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus to D-Ala-D-lactate (or D-Ala-D-serine), which binds vancomycin poorly.

cards.front: What is red man syndrome, and how is it prevented?
cards.back: An infusion reaction after rapid i.v. vancomycin. It is not an allergy: the drug directly releases histamine from mast cells, causing flushing of the face and upper body, urticaria, tachycardia and occasionally hypotension. Prevent it by infusing slowly (systemic doses over about 1 hour); GG14 adds that premedication with an antihistamine can help. It is generally not seen with teicoplanin.

cards.front: What toxicities must be watched during vancomycin therapy?
cards.back: Ototoxicity (nerve deafness, may be permanent) and dose-related nephrotoxicity, which adds to that of aminoglycosides; GG14 notes that some penicillins may increase the renal risk. Skin reactions and fall in blood pressure can occur with rapid infusion. Reduce the dose in renal insufficiency, because the drug is excreted unchanged in urine (half-life about 6 hours). Monitoring: trough levels of 15-20 mcg/mL were the older target for serious infection; GG14 states that newer guidelines target an AUC of 400-600 mg.h/L for serious MRSA infection.

cards.front: List the main uses of vancomycin.
cards.text: Systemic: {{serious MRSA}} infection; {{enterococcal endocarditis}} with an aminoglycoside in penicillin-allergic patients; empirical {{bacterial meningitis}} with a cephalosporin; surgical {{prophylaxis}} where MRSA is common or in beta-lactam allergy. Oral (not absorbed): {{C. difficile}} colitis, for which GG14 lists oral vancomycin as a drug of choice, and {{staphylococcal enterocolitis}}.

cards.front: How does linezolid differ from other protein-synthesis inhibitors?
cards.back: It is an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit at the P site and blocks formation of the initiation complex, so protein synthesis never starts. It is mainly bacteriostatic and has no cross-resistance with other antibiotic classes; enterococci can become resistant through 23S rRNA mutation. Active against MRSA, VRE and penicillin-resistant pneumococci, but not Gram-negative bacilli.

cards.front: Short note: Linezolid toxicity and interactions

points: Thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anaemia after more than 2 weeks; usually reversible
Optic and peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use (KDT: beyond about 4 weeks)
Lactic acidosis, also mainly with prolonged courses (GG14)
Weak MAO inhibitor: serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and serotonergic drugs
No cytochrome P450 interactions reported
Nausea, diarrhoea, taste disturbance; rarely rash, headache

cards.front: Why is linezolid kept in reserve, and why is it unsuitable for enterococcal endocarditis?
cards.back: It is reserved for serious drug-resistant Gram-positive infections, such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, wound infection, and infection with VRE or vancomycin-resistant MRSA, to limit resistance. Because it is bacteriostatic, it is unsuitable for enterococcal endocarditis. Dose 600 mg twice daily, oral or i.v., with no renal adjustment. In TB, KDT calls it a reserve drug for XDR-TB; GG14 states that WHO now classes it as a Group A drug for MDR-TB, and that it is part of the 6-month bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid regimen approved for XDR-TB.

cards.front: Daptomycin: mechanism, indications and key toxicity.
cards.back: A lipopeptide whose lipid tail inserts into the bacterial membrane, where molecules aggregate into pores. Potassium leaks out, the membrane depolarises, and DNA, RNA and protein synthesis stop. It is bactericidal only against Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA and VRE. Indicated for complicated skin infections and S. aureus bacteraemia, not pneumonia. Dose 4 mg/kg daily for skin infection and 6 mg/kg daily for bacteraemia or endocarditis. Toxicity: myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins; eosinophilic pneumonia after more than 2 weeks.

cards.front: Which drugs are options for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE)?
cards.text: Options named in the chapter include {{linezolid}}, {{daptomycin}}, {{tigecycline}} and {{quinupristin-dalfopristin}}; the last is not active against {{E. faecalis}}, and {{teicoplanin}} works only on some VRE strains.

cards.front: How do polymyxin B and colistin kill Gram-negative bacteria?
cards.back: They are cationic polypeptides with a detergent-like action. They bind membrane phospholipids, distort the membrane and form pseudopores, so ions and amino acids leak out; polymyxin B also binds and inactivates the lipid A of endotoxin. They are rapidly bactericidal against Gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter and Enterobacterales. Proteus, Serratia and Neisseria are not inhibited, and GG14 adds that Stenotrophomonas and Burkholderia are usually resistant. Resistance is uncommon but, as GG14 notes, has emerged during treatment of extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter and Klebsiella.

cards.front: Where are polymyxin B and colistin used, and how has their systemic role changed?
cards.back: They are not absorbed from the gut or from mucous membranes, so they are used topically (skin, burns, otitis externa, eye) and oral colistin has been used for Gram-negative bacillary diarrhoea in infants. KDT notes they were abandoned for systemic use because of toxicity. GG14 states that their systemic use has increased with the rise of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria: they are now given i.v. only for serious infection with organisms resistant to other effective drugs, usually in combination, and are less effective than newer agents such as ceftazidime-avibactam.

cards.front: Bacitracin, mupirocin and fusidic acid: where are these topical agents used?
cards.text: {{Bacitracin}} is topical only, for wounds and eyes (kidney-toxic if given systemically); {{mupirocin}} treats impetigo and small wounds; {{fusidic acid}} treats penicillinase-producing staphylococcal boils and skin infection.

cards.front: How does nitrofurantoin act, and why has its use narrowed?
cards.back: Bacterial nitroreductases convert it into reactive intermediates that damage DNA and interfere with protein synthesis. It is mainly bacteriostatic but can be cidal at high concentration and in acid urine. Its broad Gram-negative activity has narrowed largely to E. coli, because of resistance; Pseudomonas and Proteus are resistant. Resistance does not emerge rapidly during treatment. It achieves antibacterial levels only in urine, not in blood or tissues.

cards.front: What is the main indication for nitrofurantoin, and what are typical doses?
cards.back: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection, not associated with prostatitis; it is now a reserve drug. Acute infection (KDT): 50 to 100 mg three times daily for 5 to 10 days, not more than 2 weeks at a time. GG14 gives 100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days for the macrocrystalline form. Suppression of recurrent cystitis: 50 mg twice daily or 100 mg at bedtime. It is unsuitable for pyelonephritis, because it does not reach kidney tissue.

cards.front: When must nitrofurantoin be avoided, and what are its main adverse effects?
cards.back: Avoid in renal failure (poor excretion and rising toxicity), in pregnancy, and in neonates. The commonest effect is gastrointestinal intolerance. Others: acute chills, fever and leucopenia; peripheral neuritis with long use; haemolytic anaemia, especially in G6PD deficiency; rarely liver damage and chronic pulmonary fibrosis. Urine turns dark brown on standing. Probenecid reduces its concentration in urine.

Lower UTI: about 3 days; pyelonephritis: 10 to 14 days, with a potent drug
Ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin (avoid in pregnancy)
Cotrimoxazole; cephalexin or cefpodoxime
Amoxicillin-clavulanate; nitrofurantoin for 5 to 7 days
Nitrofurantoin not used for pyelonephritis; parenteral options include gentamicin with a potent agent
Avoid methenamine and tetracyclines (except doxycycline); avoid potassium and acidifying agents
Bedtime cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, norfloxacin or cephalexin

cards.front: Short note: Systemic polymyxins (colistimethate and polymyxin B)

points: Serious infection with Gram-negative bacteria resistant to other effective drugs (bacteraemia, pneumonia, meningitis, cystic fibrosis)
Usually combined with another antibiotic (carbapenem, tetracycline or aminoglycoside)
Reserved for organisms resistant to newer agents such as ceftazidime-avibactam
Colistin is given i.v. as colistimethate (CMS), an inactive prodrug slowly hydrolysed to colistin; renally cleared, so the dose is reduced in renal dysfunction
Polymyxin B is active as given and cleared mainly by non-renal routes
Polymyxin B is preferred for most systemic infections; CMS for infections arising in the urinary tract
CMS can also be inhaled, or given intraventricularly for CNS infection
Dose-related nephrotoxicity from renal tubular damage, with a narrow therapeutic window
Neurotoxicity: muscle weakness, apnoea, paraesthesia, vertigo, slurred speech

cards.front: Lipoglycopeptides (telavancin, dalbavancin, oritavancin): how do they differ from vancomycin?
cards.back: Their antibacterial spectrum is broadly similar to vancomycin, and they are also active against some vancomycin-resistant enterococci. Dalbavancin and oritavancin are highly protein bound with a terminal half-life of about 10 days, so a single dose (or two doses a week apart) treats skin and soft-tissue infection. Telavancin is given once daily and was as effective as vancomycin in hospital-acquired Gram-positive pneumonia, but it may be more nephrotoxic than vancomycin. Oritavancin can affect warfarin, so monitor if they are combined.

cards.front: Newer tetracycline congeners designed to overcome resistance
cards.text: Tetracycline congeners engineered to overcome resistance include the glycylcycline {{tigecycline}}, the fluorocycline {{eravacycline}} and the aminomethylcycline {{omadacycline}}. Tigecycline and eravacycline are given only {{intravenously}}, while omadacycline can be given orally or i.v.; omadacycline is approved for community-acquired bacterial {{pneumonia}}.
